questions.q: A service receives 86.4 million requests per day, evenly spread. What is the approximate average QPS?
questions.explanation: A day holds 86,400 seconds, so 86.4 million requests divide out to about 1,000 QPS. The 86,400 option confuses the seconds-per-day constant with the rate.

questions.q: Roughly how long does a single main-memory (RAM) reference take on modern hardware?
questions.explanation: A DRAM reference costs roughly 100 ns in the standard latency numbers. About 1 ns is an L1 cache hit, and 10 ms is closer to a spinning-disk seek.

questions.q: 2^20 bytes is closest to which size?
questions.explanation: Each factor of 2^10 is about a thousand, so 2^20 is roughly a million bytes, or 1 MB. 2^30 would be the gigabyte.

questions.q: Ten million users each upload one 2 MB photo daily. Approximate new storage per day?
questions.explanation: 10 million times 2 MB is 20 million MB, which is 20 TB per day. Watch the factor of a thousand between MB, GB, and TB.

questions.q: What is a typical network round-trip time within a single data center?
questions.explanation: Intra-datacenter round trips are sub-millisecond, around 0.5 ms. Tens of milliseconds is what you expect across regions or continents.

questions.q: Which is a reasonable figure for reading 1 MB sequentially from an SSD?
questions.explanation: At roughly 1 GB/s of sequential SSD throughput, 1 MB takes about 1 ms. A microsecond would imply terabytes per second, which no SSD delivers.

questions.q: A platform stores 500 million short posts daily at about 200 bytes of text each. Approximate daily text storage?
questions.explanation: 5 x 10^8 posts times 200 bytes is 10^11 bytes, about 100 GB per day. Text is cheap; media would dominate this number.

questions.q: Why estimate peak QPS separately from average QPS?
options: Peak equals average in any well-designed system
Averages cannot be computed from daily totals
Capacity must handle bursts, often 2-10x the average
Peak QPS only matters for storage sizing, not compute capacity
questions.explanation: Traffic is bursty by time of day and events, so capacity sized to the average will fail during peaks that run several times higher. Peak drives compute, not just storage.

questions.q: A pastebin gets 1 million new pastes daily, averaging 10 KB, retained for 5 years. Approximate total storage needed?
questions.explanation: Daily volume is 10 GB, and 5 years is about 1,825 days, giving roughly 18 TB. Dropping or adding a factor of ten here is the classic slip.

questions.q: A service must serve 30,000 QPS; each app server handles 1,000 QPS at a 70% utilization target. Servers needed?
questions.explanation: Usable capacity per server is 700 QPS, so 30,000 divided by 700 is about 43. Answering 30 ignores the headroom the utilization target reserves.

questions.q: A service does 10,000 QPS with 100 KB average responses. Approximate egress bandwidth?
questions.explanation: 10,000 times 100 KB is 1,000,000 KB per second, which is about 1 GB/s. That is roughly 8 Gbps of network, enough to matter for NIC sizing.

questions.q: A network round trip between the US and Europe is closest to?
questions.explanation: Transatlantic round trips land near 100 ms once fiber speed and routing overhead are included. Speed of light alone sets a floor of several tens of milliseconds.

questions.q: A URL shortener uses 7-character base-62 IDs. Roughly how many unique IDs are possible?
questions.explanation: 62^7 is about 3.5 x 10^12, so seven base-62 characters cover trillions of keys. That is ample headroom for decades of typical shortener traffic.

questions.q: 1 billion users, 1% concurrently connected over WebSockets, 100,000 connections per server. Approximately how many servers?
questions.explanation: 1% of a billion is 10 million concurrent connections, and dividing by 100,000 per server gives about 100 servers. Real deployments add more for redundancy and headroom.

questions.q: Which ordering of typical latencies is correct, smallest first?
options: Disk seek < RAM read < same-datacenter RTT
RAM read < disk seek < L1 cache hit
Same-datacenter RTT < RAM read < L1 cache hit
L1 cache hit < RAM read < disk seek
questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs about 1 ns for L1, 100 ns for RAM, and milliseconds for a disk seek. Each step down the memory hierarchy costs orders of magnitude more.

questions.q: 200 million daily active users each make 50 read requests per day. Approximate average read QPS?
questions.explanation: That is 10 billion reads per day, and dividing by 86,400 seconds gives roughly 115,000 QPS. Peak traffic would run several times higher than this average.

questions.q: A cache serves 90% of reads at 1 ms; misses go on to the database at 10 ms. Approximate average read latency?
questions.explanation: The weighted mean is 0.9 x 1 plus 0.1 x 10, which is 1.9 ms, about 2 ms. Note the 10% of misses contribute as much as all the hits combined.

questions.q: 1 TB of 1 KB records gets a per-record index entry of 100 bytes. Total index overhead?
questions.explanation: 1 TB of 1 KB records is about a billion records, and a billion 100-byte entries is roughly 100 GB. That is 10% overhead, often too large to keep fully in RAM.

questions.q: Why do p99 latency targets matter more than averages for pages with large backend fanout?
options: Averages cannot be measured reliably at scale
p99 is by definition 99 times the average
Fanout automatically reduces tail latency by parallelizing the calls
With many parallel calls, most page loads include at least one slow backend response
questions.explanation: A page waiting on 100 parallel calls each with a 1% slow tail almost always hits at least one, so the tail becomes the typical user experience. Parallelism spreads tail latency rather than hiding it.

questions.q: A log partition sustains about 10 MB/s. You must ingest 1 GB/s with 2x headroom. Minimum partitions?
questions.explanation: 2x headroom means provisioning for 2 GB/s, and 2,000 MB/s divided by 10 MB/s per partition is 200. Answering 100 forgets to apply the headroom factor.
